headline: Iran's Supreme National Security Council has outlined six conditions it says must be met before the Strait of Hormuz will be reopened to commercial shipping: 1. Cease all threats and insults toward Iran. 2. Permanently end what Iran describes as its "war of aggression" against Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Iraq, and Yemen. 3. Lift the naval blockade of Iran and withdraw all U.S. naval and air forces operating around the country. 4. Pay reparations for damage caused during the conflict. 5. Lift all sanctions imposed on Iran. 6. "Unconditionally" release all frozen Iranian assets. The demands underscore the significant gap that remains between the two sides. Several of the conditions, including ending the U.S. military presence in the region, lifting sanctions, and paying reparations, would represent major shifts in longstanding U.S. policy, making a near term resolution to the Strait of Hormuz crisis appear unlikely.

headline: The Department of War has revoked former Secretary of the Air Force Frank Kendall's eligibility to access classified information and his ability to hold any sensitive Department of War position, citing an alleged "unauthorized disclosure of classified information regarding Air Force One's capabilities to a media outlet." Kendall served as Secretary of the Air Force from July 28, 2021, until January 20, 2025. While the Department of War has not identified the specific disclosure at issue, the action comes days after Kendall publicly commented on the capabilities of the VC-25B "Bridge" aircraft (the interim presidential aircraft converted from a Qatari-donated Boeing 747) during media reporting comparing it to the existing VC-25A fleet. Those reports highlighted that the Bridge aircraft lacks several capabilities of the legacy Air Force One fleet and will undergo additional upgrades. At this time, it remains unclear whether the revocation is directly related to those comments or to a separate alleged disclosure.

headline: U.S. intelligence has reportedly linked the explosive-laden drone discovered at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport this week to the Russian government, according to The Wall Street Journal. The drone was discovered Tuesday night inside a secure area of the airport, just meters from a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft, carrying what German investigators reportedly determined was an explosive device with a defective detonator that failed to function. The discovery forced the airport to suspend operations overnight. Authorities are also investigating a second suspected drone that a DHL cargo aircraft reportedly struck after executing a go-around due to the airport closure, with the aircraft later landing safely despite damage to its nose. The development comes one day after The Wall Street Journal reported that new U.S. intelligence assessments warn Vladimir Putin could test NATO's resolve through limited attacks ranging from sabotage and cyber operations to a small-scale incursion into alliance territory. Western officials have increasingly warned that Russia is conducting probing operations against NATO infrastructure, with previous incidents including drones entering Romanian airspace and Russian missiles landing in Poland.

headline: Earlier today, the U.S. Senate passed Senate Bill 5025, the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026”, by a margin of 86-11 sending the bill to the U.S. House of Representatives. Key provisions include: • Up to 500% tariffs on goods imported directly from Russia. • Up to 100% tariffs on imports from the largest purchasers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, as well as countries determined to be facilitating Russian sanctions evasion. • Expanded sanctions targeting Russian government officials, banks, energy companies, vessels involved in sanctions evasion, and entities supporting Russia's defense industrial base. • New restrictions on investment in Russia, Russian energy exports, uranium imports, sovereign debt purchases, and access to international financial messaging systems. If enacted, the legislation would represent one of the most comprehensive U.S. sanctions packages against Russia since the start of the war in Ukraine, while also increasing economic pressure on third countries that continue purchasing Russian energy.

headline: The Bahamas-flagged, Qatar-owned liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier Al Areesh appears to be approaching the U.S. naval blockade line at the entrance to the Gulf of Oman for a third time, after twice previously reversing course or loitering near the line without exiting the Gulf. The Al Areesh departed Qatar's Ras Laffan LNG terminal and transited the Strait of Hormuz outbound on July 29, utilizing Iran's traffic separation scheme, according to publicly available AIS tracking data from http://MarineTraffic.com. Its continued inability to proceed beyond the apparent blockade line is notable because the vessel does not appear to have loaded cargo in Iran or be associated with an Iranian port, and therefore does not appear to fit the publicly understood criteria for vessels subject to the U.S. naval blockade. It remains unclear whether the vessel's unusual movements are the result of instructions from its owner or operator, operational considerations, or direction from U.S. forces.
summary: The Bahamas-flagged, Qatar-owned liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier Al Areesh appears to be approaching the U.S. naval blockade line at the entrance to the Gulf of Oman for a third time, after twice previously reversing course or loitering near the line without exiting the Gulf.

headline: ADNOC says 15 of its vessels have been attacked by Iranian missiles or drones since the start of the war, including three this week, underscoring the continued risks to commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz. According to ADNOC, one crew member has been killed and 20 others injured as the company works to keep crude oil, LNG and refined products flowing despite repeated attacks. Before the war, the Strait of Hormuz carried roughly 20% of global oil consumption, but vessel attacks have driven up insurance and freight costs while discouraging some shipowners from entering the Persian Gulf. Despite the security environment, ADNOC is expanding its fleet, announcing the acquisition of 11 VLCC and VLGC vessels worth approximately $1.3 billion to support future export capacity.

headline: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have signed the 'Mecca Joint Defence Agreement', pledging that an armed attack on one will be treated as an attack on all, creating a new trilateral security framework amid the expanding Middle East conflict. The agreement stops short of detailing automatic military obligations, but it formalizes closer defense coordination between three of the Muslim world's most influential militaries. Saudi Arabia has come under repeated Iranian attacks since the start of Operation Epic Fury, Turkey fields NATO's second-largest military, and Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim-majority nation. The pact follows nearly a year of negotiations and reflects growing concern that regional states may need to rely more on their own security architecture as the Iran conflict continues to threaten Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping. Turkish and Saudi officials stressed the agreement is defensive in nature and is not directed at any specific country.
